rationale: Extracting information from minds loosely points to brain decoding. The passage has no specific thought or image reconstruction, and the mechanism is unspecified.
Probing a mind for thoughts points toward brain decoding, but no mechanism is given. fMRI movie reconstruction is far more limited.
A probe that extracts memories directly is the right general idea, but it is vague. The real work reconstructed only approximate viewed video.
A deep-probe device reading a person is evocative of brain decoding with no mechanism. The real development is far more limited.
Predicting actions seconds ahead from muscular and nervous preparation is not reading thoughts or images. It only loosely points toward neural decoding.
A shielded room like those used for encephalographic analysis, with mental activity analyzed, loosely resembles brain scanning. It does not say specific thoughts or images are read.
The machine detects that a mind is being read, which is not reading a person's thoughts.
The device cannot detect telepathy or mind-reading, which is not thought decoding.
Electrical brain patterns are read remotely by radio waves, so the function of reading thoughts matches. fMRI works by different physics and is not remote.
A helmet scan reading someone's psychology loosely resembles brain scanning. It does not say thoughts or images are decoded.
Detecting brain waves that carry individual words matches reading specific thoughts from the brain. It resembles EEG sensing but gives no mechanism for the decoding.
A machine that records the audience's thought waves and synthesizes them is brain-signal reconstruction. The mechanism is vague and the context is entertainment.
A sign advertising innermost thoughts revealed describes no technology.
A tiny remote-controlled proxy robot via brain helmets points to micro-scale robots only loosely. Real DNA robots are autonomous molecular machines.
Micro-robots with electron vision are evocative of microscopic machines. They are remotely driven and far larger than DNA nanomachines.
A microscopic electronic brain is only loosely a microscopic robot. Real molecular robots have no such intelligence.
An implanted device reading nerve impulses of the speech organs to reconstruct speech is a neural interface. It does not restore hearing the way the cochlear implant does.
A skull-mounted bone-conduction speaker for silent communication with an implanted device is body-joined electronics. It loosely echoes sensory augmentation, not a cochlear implant.
A concealed implant behind the ear is an electronic body device, loosely related to cochlear implants. The passage gives no sensory restoration function.
The quote says only that it was a neurological instrument and not a psychologist. It describes no sense or ability restored.
Scanning nearby people's nervous systems is not restoring or extending the host's sense through a cochlear implant.
A person acting as a living calculator is a mental feat with no implanted device.
Electronic brains inserted and connected to neural paths loosely echo neural implants extending ability. The cochlear implant restores hearing, which is a different function.
Brain implants absorbing information to replace memorization extend memory in a way no cochlear implant does. They point in the same direction only loosely.
A control panel for a power plant is not an implant.
A surgically implanted electronic brain is a neural implant in broad terms. Its function of computing tactics differs from restoring a sense.
An implant sensing nerve changes to send a signal resembles neural interfaces loosely. Its teleport trigger function differs from cochlear sensory restoration.
A helmet linking the commander to the ship is a human-machine link that is not implanted. It is evocative only.
A calculating machine combined with a typewriter producing accounts and invoices matches automating clerical accounting. LEO's bakery valuations are a similar function, but the mechanism is vague.
Tape machines with electronic eyes that select words to speak are not character recognition for sorting or data entry.
Robots scanning addresses photoelectrically to sort mail match the USPS OCR sorter. The passage does not say characters are read.
A scanner that turns book pages is a page-reading device, loosely related. No character recognition is described.
A machine that reads typewriting directly without coded cards matches optical reading of printed text. The insurance context differs from mail sorting.
Mail sorters with scanning elements are mentioned only in passing. The passage gives no reading mechanism.
Customs scanners and paper-checkers are evocative of automated document reading. Nothing says characters are read.
Machine sifting of wreckage for registration plates fed to central records points loosely at automated plate reading. Nothing is said about optical reading.
Fingers flashing over keys of a computer beside a chair does not show a personal computer owned for individual use.
A keyboard electro-reckoner for complex calculations is a desk machine, not a small battery-powered personal device.
A cube with columns of buttons that computes is a hand-operated calculating device, loosely like a pocket calculator. No small personal portable function is stated.
A passing remark that a mechanism could be adapted for a calculator describes no calculator.
A Minicalculator used by statisticians matches a compact calculator. The portability and personal ownership are not stated.
Computing a route on an electronic calculator names the device and its function. It does not say the device is small or personal.
Spoken queries answered by a book with locations and plans match question answering by a knowledge store. Breadth and open-domain ability are not shown.
Aliens cracking problems into formulae are a different thing from a knowledge-holding machine.
A machine that weighs all stored information to answer coded problems matches the question-answering function. Input is coded rather than ordinary language, and the mechanism is vague.
Using logic computers to compute the truth is a loose pointer to a question-answering machine. No answering of factual questions is described.
Asking a logic computer about its own security is not factual question answering.
A machine-brain that weighs facts and gives an answer is a general pointer to question answering. It lacks any question and answer specifics.
A giant public computer that is like a mother figure is evocative only. It does not state question answering.
Any question is submitted and answered by a machine brain, matching question answering in function. Input is by microtape, not ordinary language, and the answering is not shown.
A colossal machine brain that answers all questions matches the function of question answering. No mechanism is given.
A talking machine registrar with an air of petulance is only loosely a question-answering computer. Answering from data is not in the quote.
The quote concerns energy-beings that outperform a calculator, not a computer.
A machine that answers anything, given a legitimate question, matches the function. No mechanism or language interface is stated.
A computer receives an entered problem and replies in text, such as INSUFFICIENT DATA. The question-answering function matches, but the knowledge base and language mechanism are vague.
A giant brain that can be asked questions as a research oracle matches the question-answering function. The mechanism and language interface are not detailed.
A large computer integrating the sciences loosely points at a broad knowledge machine. No question answering is stated.
Machines that answer the problems of daily life loosely suggest question answering. The passage is mostly about prophecy.
A giant computer financed by a consortium and relied on by agencies is evocative of an answering machine. No question answering is stated.
A computer that outputs an answer on tape is a generic answering machine. It does not show breadth of knowledge or natural-language questions.
A computer that knows what it is talking about is only loosely an answering machine. No questions are described.
An information center that answers any question matches the function, but the machine is a human and robot institution. No computer mechanism is shown.
A master computer is described by appearance only. Answering natural-language questions comes from the claim, not the quote.
A device that hears questions and answers from a huge microtape memory matches spoken question answering over large stored knowledge. It is a children's interpreter and the mechanism is thin.
A computer composes recorded words to answer an almost infinite number of questions, matching spoken question answering. Knowledge breadth is not stated and the mechanism is a crude concatenation.
A larger master computer that queries are referred to loosely suggests a query-answering system. The quote shows no answering.
An information robot in a kiosk is evocative of an information machine. The quote gives no answering of questions.
An oracle machine that responds to a person's questions is loosely question answering. The quote describes restricting access, not capability.
A machine oracle that answers any question promptly and completely matches the function. No mechanism is given.
A machine that identifies aliens and issues orders is not question answering.
An information bank of a policy machine implies a queryable database. The quote shows no answering of questions.
Feeding all information to a Brain to get an answer loosely suggests a question-answering system. The coded inputs and decision-making role differ.
A brain charged with a civilization's knowledge points at a knowledge-holding computer. Answering questions is not stated.
Requesting a horoscope from a computer is not factual question answering.
A station computer is said to produce results by selection. This loosely suggests an information store but is not question answering.
A computer holding all human knowledge, scanning and reasoning, matches broad-knowledge answering. Questions in ordinary language are not stated.
Faking computation results with a dummy describes a hoax, not question answering.
Detector stations whose tracks display automatically on a whole-Earth map match sensor-driven live display. The passage does not name a computer.
A table-map with circles marking the air-cities' positions is a plot display. Live updating and sensing are not stated.
A space-chart on the wall is a display of positions. Live tracking is not stated in the quote.
A telechart is a navigation display plate. Nothing in the quote says positions are live or computer-driven.
A chart showing glowing circles and ship-dots moving toward a goal matches a live positions display. Sensors and a computer are not stated.
A table-map on which red circles automatically show the position of air-cities matches a live tracking display. The objects are fictional, with no stated computer or radar.
A metal plate representing the nearby heavens is a map-like display. It does not say live tracking.
Spark and pinpoint lights showing positions of the ship and other bodies match a position display. Live detection is only in the claim.
Punched coordinates make a point appear in a galaxy tank. This is a manual locator display, not live tracking.
A huge tank with millions of lights moving matches a large live tracking display. The sensor and computer mechanism is not stated.
Pointing a device at a light yields a number, which describes identification rather than the situation display.
A tank ringed by a million-plug board is a console loosely related to a command display. The quote says nothing of live positions.
A tank showing the disposition of every enemy unit matches a tactical positions display. Real-time sensing is implied but not stated.
A tactical tank fed by telepathic summarizers is a tactical display. The sensor and computer mechanism is different.
The quote gives only the size of a tank, with no display function.
A transparent hull with glowing filaments tracing mechanism status is a live status display. It shows machine state, not positions of tracked objects.
World and space maps with colored symbols are command displays. Live tracking is not stated in the quote.
A circular graph with pulsing lines is a display. Tracking is only in the claim.
The quote describes only a command ship carrying the Brains.
A large 3-D chart of a star system is a map-like display. It is not stated to be live.
An autoscanner on a radar-like device that clangs at blips on screens matches radar contacts on a screen with automatic detection. It has no plotting of positions or computer network.
A chart projection screen showing their position is a position display. The quote does not say live tracking or sensing.
A tri-dim chart filling a room is a display. It does not state tracking.
A realistic electronic map that seems to breathe with cities is evocative of a live situational map. The mechanism is vague.
The speaker says robots cannot be manufactured, which is the opposite of an industry.
Robots that replace human labor are a pointer to industrial robot use. No manufacturing industry or product sale is described.
One animated dummy proposing to make others is not a commercial industry.
A trade-marked robot from Spurgin's Robots implies a commercial robot maker. The humanoid woman context differs from industrial arms.
Quinby's function-shaped robots suggest a maker but give no industry or sales.
The quote only mentions the invention of the mechanical brain.
A corporation turning out thousands of industrial robots matches robot manufacturing as a commercial industry. The off-world setting differs.
Populating a town with robots shows no manufacturing industry.
Rows of rusting robot populations show no robot-making business.
A purchased standard-model all-around robot worker implies a product sold on the market. No manufacturer or manufacturing process is described.
A humandroid factory with a foreman matches factory production of robots. Humanlike androids differ from real industrial robots.
A model of which 25 are under construction indicates limited manufacture. No sales are stated.
Specialist models replacing general-purpose ones implies a market with differing robot models. No manufacturing detail is given.
Obsolete robots replaced by newer generations is a story about robots' fate, not an industry.
Model I robots built to a buyer's specifications of size, color and personality match a commercial robot product line. They are humanoid, with customization far beyond real early robots.
Robots offered with selectable intelligence level imply a commercial product catalogue. The levels of autonomy are fictional.
A robotics business is implied by the quote about someone branching into robotics. Little else is said.
A company built a thousand servitor models, implying robot manufacture. They were experimental, and sale is not stated.
Numbered robot types imply mass production. No commercial industry is described.
